record.title: Cameras, Safes, and Smart Habits: Residential Burglary Prevention Tips
record.locator: Basics; valuables; camera placement; security assessment
record.finding: Supports locks, reinforced strike plates, secured garages, maintained sightlines, motion lighting, protected valuables and thoughtful camera coverage. It offers residential assessments; no percentage or post-collapse deterrence guarantee is supplied.

record.title: False Alarm and Security Systems
record.locator: False alarm prevention; power interruptions; user training
record.finding: Outages, low batteries, weather and user errors can trigger false alarms. Maintain contacts/batteries and teach users operation/cancellation. Local registration and response rules apply; backup power is finite, not a promise of instant police arrival.

record.title: 13VAC5-52-220: Means of Egress
record.finding: Required exits and rescue openings must remain usable under the applicable building code. Bars/grilles over required rescue openings must release from inside without keys/tools or excessive force. Do not infer every window is a required opening or every residential lock has the same rule.

record.title: Model Jury Instructions — Criminal, Release26
record.finding: Instruction33.800 describes without-fault self-defense in terms of reasonable imminent fear of death/great bodily harm and no more force than reasonably necessary.33.810 has different at-fault conditions. This is a legal limit, not a complete opinion on a household incident or permission to shoot over property.

record.title: Code18.2-51: Bodily injury with intent to maim, disable or kill
record.finding: Virginia criminalizes specified malicious or unlawful bodily injury with the stated intent. Reviewer applies this as a warning against injurious traps; the statute is not a trap-design rule or a complete determination of liability in a hypothetical disaster.

record.title: Preventing Firearm Injury and Death
record.finding: Hiding or placing firearms out of reach is not secure storage. Locked storage helps prevent unauthorized access; unloaded locked guns and separately secured ammunition are emphasized. This does not validate firearm selection, use-of-force tactics or a weapon-filled family refuge.

record.title: How To Secure Your Home Security Cameras
record.finding: Connected cameras require protected accounts/networks, updates, encryption, appropriate permissions and consideration of remote-viewing privacy. Convenience is not immunity from compromise or outage.

record.title: Hold Mail Service
record.finding: USPS offers eligible-address mail holding for3–30days, with identity verification for online requests. This verifies availability of the service, not crime reduction or indefinite holding.

record.title: Safety and Security Window Films brochure
record.finding: Properly applied films may retain shards and delay intrusion under stated conditions; manufacturer disclaims bullet resistance and guaranteed prevention of injury or entry. Product and installation selection need professional assessment.

record.publisher: Office of the Federal Register / CPSC
record.title: 16CFR1201.1: Architectural glazing scope
record.finding: Safety-glazing requirements apply to specified architectural products including doors and patio-type sliding doors. Scope, material, manufacture and application matter. This does not mandate acrylic in every window or establish burglary/ballistic resistance.

record.title: Testing and Certification for Bullet-Resistant Materials
record.finding: UL752 evaluates specified barrier materials/assemblies for penetration, fragments and spalling under defined ballistic conditions. No household sandbag pile or ordinary metal door becomes rated merely by material name; no book assembly was tested.

record.title: What to Expect
record.finding: Contact before digging or driving landscaping/fence supports, wait for the applicable process and account for private utilities that member locates do not mark. This constrains lawful fencing and burial projects, not injurious traps.

record.title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply
record.finding: Home-filled drinking water needs suitable containers, dates, rotation and cool storage away from sunlight/toxic substances. A hiding place or buried container does not prove safe water or household coverage.

record.title: Expiration Dates — Questions and Answers
record.finding: Labeled storage and expiry matter. Temperature, humidity and light affect stability; controlled federal-stockpile extensions do not establish a household product’s condition. Buried or concealed medicines are not automatically safely stored.

record.title: Carbon Monoxide Hazard: Using a Generator
record.finding: Generator exhaust can kill; never run a generator indoors, in a garage or carport. Theft protection or anchoring must not override ventilation and safe operating location.

record.title: Euphorbia milii — Crown of Thorns
record.finding: Latex sap can injure skin/eyes and ingestion causes irritation; keep away from children/pets. This is one species associated with the common name, not proof of the author’s botanical intent or Virginia outdoor suitability.

record.title: Japanese Barberry
record.finding: Japanese barberry is identified as invasive in Virginia regions and thorns can injure pedestrians. The book’s unspecific barberry label does not identify a cultivar/species; do not treat all barberries as identical.

record.title: Residential Fences and Walls
record.finding: Fence height/location and certain permits depend on lot, use and exceptions. This county summary illustrates local constraints only; household jurisdiction, parcel and lawful fence design are unknown.

record.title: What to do During a Tornado
record.finding: Tornado shelter choices favor a basement, safe room or suitable interior room away from windows; a shed is not a substitute. Intrusion hiding places are not automatically weather shelters.

record.title: Riot Control Agents
record.locator: Background; signs and symptoms; closed settings
record.finding: Pepper spray and related irritants can injure eyes/airways/skin; severe and potentially fatal effects can occur with major/prolonged exposure, especially enclosed settings. Non-lethal is not a harmlessness guarantee.

record.title: Resolve to be Ready for Emergencies
record.finding: Supports neighbor communication, emergency planning, alerts, documents and device backup power. It does not endorse vigilantism, armed neighborhood control or assuming all responders are absent.

record.title: Predictions are not a local threat assessment
record.guidance: No evidence establishes inevitable collapse, universal looting, a three-second criminal decision,90percent superiority or that every intruder will pass this home. Plan for actual hazards and official alerts; limited burglary-prevention principles do not validate disaster forecasts.

record.title: Security must preserve escape and rescue
record.guidance: Do not permanently block required exits/rescue openings with bars, boards, furniture, jammers, grilles or stockpiles. Check applicable code, releases, clear opening and each person’s ability to escape; obtain qualified local review.

record.title: Door strength is an assembly question
record.guidance: Door leaf, frame, strike, hinges, anchorage, installation and applicable fire/accessibility rules matter. Material or a three-inch screw alone is not a forced-entry or ballistic rating. No universal replacement of every wooden door is justified.

record.title: Glazing and film need specified performance
record.guidance: Select a compatible complete assembly for impact, safety glazing, frame retention and required opening operation. Acrylic, laminated glass and film are not interchangeable; no universal all-window acrylic retrofit or bullet resistance established.16CFR1201covers specified products, not every window indiscriminately.

record.title: Cameras have operational and privacy dependencies
record.guidance: Test fields of view, tamper exposure, night images, local recording, retention, power, network and remote access. Protect accounts/updates/permissions. Eye-level mounting and wide view do not guarantee useful identification; cloud access is not outage independence.

record.title: Alarm and monitoring response are conditional
record.guidance: Test sensors and alert delivery with the provider, train all users, maintain batteries/contacts and confirm jurisdictional registration, cancellation and response policies. No sensor threshold eliminates all false alarms; no panic/duress feature guarantees silent immediate police response.

record.title: Deterrence claims need measured limits
record.guidance: Lights, signs, recorded barking, fake cameras and unpredictable activity do not certify crime prevention. Match safe visibility and neighbors’ needs; retain the book’s power-dependence caveats and its later conflicting warning about fake defenses.

record.title: Neighborhood cooperation is observation and mutual aid
record.guidance: Use trusted communication, reporting, check-ins and official channels. No armed patrol, discriminatory suspicion, improvised checkpoint or street enclosure follows from neighborhood watch. A disaster does not prove police or emergency help cannot be contacted.

record.title: Trip-line alarms are not validated safety systems
record.guidance: No detection range, false-alarm rate, audibility, weather or accessible-route test is provided. Avoid trip/entanglement hazards to household, visitors and responders. Use a safe commercial or professionally assessed alert option rather than copy this perimeter outline.

record.title: Reject devices intended to injure entrants
record.guidance: Do not install nail boards, bear traps, stake pits or projecting injury stakes against people, whether hidden or visible. They cannot distinguish a threat from children, neighbors or rescuers. Training, warnings or waiting for an outage does not establish legal permission or safety; use noninjurious barriers and alerts.

record.title: Property defense is not automatic authority for lethal force
record.guidance: Trespass, theft, a warning sign or an assumed collapse is not blanket permission to shoot. Virginia self-defense depends on imminent danger and circumstances; seek qualified legal/training guidance. No gun selection, firing position, funnel, fake-cover or disorientation-to-shoot tactic is approved.

record.title: Hidden weapons are not secure storage
record.guidance: Prevent unauthorized access with appropriate locked storage and safe handling; concealment, drawers, bedroom avoidance or a secret room alone is insufficient. Household needs do not establish a requirement to buy or stock every listed weapon.

record.title: Less-lethal tools still have risks
record.guidance: Pepper spray, electric weapons and ordinary tools can seriously injure people and depend on lawful possession/use, training and context. Non-lethal wording is not a safety guarantee. Do not repurpose fire-safety equipment into a required weapon kit.

record.title: Sandbags are not certified ballistic cover
record.guidance: No bag fill, thickness, projectile, angle, fragments, stability, floor-load or tested assembly evidence is provided. Do not rely on an improvised pile for bullet protection or use it to block escape; obtain qualified structural/security advice if needed.

record.title: A refuge is hazard-specific occupied space
record.guidance: An attic, closet, basement, concealed stair compartment or secret entrance does not establish safe occupancy for five people for72hours. Assess structure, fire/egress, ventilation, temperature, sanitation, access, communications and supervision. Intrusion refuge, storm safe room and long-term shelter are distinct.

record.title: Store essentials for condition and access, not concealment alone
record.guidance: Maintain labeled medicine conditions, potable-water containers/rotation, food-specific storage, household inventory and safe access. Soil, walls, appliances, sheds and underfloor spaces need assessment; hidden or diversified supplies are not proven usable. Preserve egress and child protection.

record.title: Fences need lawful siting and safe access
record.guidance: Check actual boundaries, easements, zoning/HOA restrictions, permits, gate/egress and emergency access. Arrange utility locating and private-line checks before digging/driving posts. Fairfax County examples do not establish this household’s rules; no injury perimeter authorized.

record.title: Plants require identity and suitability
record.guidance: Resolve species/cultivar, local invasive status, climate, mature size, thorns, sap toxicity and access needs. Generic barberry is not proof of Japanese barberry; crown of thorn may refer to hazardous Euphorbia milii. Preserve Quincy as printed rather than silently naming quince.

record.title: Concealment and burglary probabilities are not proven
record.guidance: No study establishes first-searched rooms, laundry-room immunity, hidden-key security or guaranteed safe concealment. Use appropriate secured storage and controlled trusted access rather than rely on novel hiding places.

record.title: Anchor equipment without creating a new hazard
record.guidance: Security chains/anchors must preserve equipment instructions, generator exhaust safety, electrical/fire clearances and evacuation access. Never run a generator in a garage or indoors to protect it from theft.

record.title: Privacy and perimeter visibility have tradeoffs
record.guidance: Opaque fences, thorny screening and privacy curtains may conflict with sightlines, access or lighting. Assess the actual site; neither high opacity nor complete openness is universally safest.

record.title: Keep mail/package arrangements realistic
record.guidance: Use eligible USPS mail holds within service limits, trusted retrieval and carrier-specific package options. Doorbell surveillance does not guarantee theft prevention, and extended absence does not make unlimited holding available.

record.title: Warning signs do not confer powers
record.guidance: Ordinary lawful property notices differ from threats to shoot or a fabricated quarantine notice. No sign creates authority to injure, impersonate public-health restrictions or deny emergency access; deterrence is unmeasured.

record.title: A sensor does not replace a response plan
record.guidance: Determine safe verification, emergency contact, accessible retreat/exit and household accountability before confronting activity. Do not investigate every perimeter alert alone or assume an alarm identifies a hostile person.

12 
Consider the following tips: 
• Illuminate all entry points, including front and back doors, garage 
entrances, and windows. Use bright, energy -efficient LED bulbs for 
enhanced visibility. 
• Position lights strategically to eliminate shadows and blind spots 
around your property. 
• Use motion-sensor lights to 
surprise and startle 
potential intruders. This 
sudden activation draws 
attention and increases the 
likelihood of detection. 
• Ensure the lighting fixtures 
are out of reach and 
tamper-proof to prevent criminals from disabling or damaging them. 
• Regularly check and replace burnt -out bulbs to maintain the 
effectiveness of your lighting system. 
• Take note that this may not be viable following an EMP attack or solar 
flare where the power grid has been knocked out, but it is something

access. Window locks should be sturdy and positioned correctly to

peephole or video doorbell 
to identify visitors before 
opening the door. This 
allows you to verify the 
person's identity without 
compromising your safety.

doors with security film or 
laminated glass, making it harder for looters to break the glass and

That’s because maintaining good visibility around your property can 
discourage looters. Consider these landscaping tips: 
• Trim bushes and hedges near windows and entry points to eliminate 
potential hiding spots for intruders. Keep shrubs below window level 
for an unobstructed view. 
• Choose plants with thorny or prickly foliage near vulnerable areas to 
create a natural deterrent. 
• Keep trees and shrubs well-maintained to enhance visibility from the 
street and neighboring properties. Overgrown vegetation can provide 
cover for looters. 
• Remove any large objects, such as ladders or tools, from your yard 
that could assist intruders in gaining access to your home. 
Valuables Concealment 
Keeping valuable items out of sight can reduce the temptation for burglars.  
Use these strategies: 
• Close blinds or curtains at night to prevent outsiders from peeking 
inside and seeing valuable possessions. Use curtains or blinds that 
are opaque or have a reflective backing for maximum privacy. 
• Avoid displaying expensive items, such as electronics or jewelry, in 
plain view from windows. Store them in secure locations or use 
curtains or blinds to obstruct visibility. 
• Dispose of packaging discreetly, especially for high -value items. 
Break down boxes and place them inside garbage bags to prevent 
potential looters from noticing recent purchases. Consider recycling 
or taking packaging to a recycling center instead of leavi ng it 
curbside.

8. Sirens and Strobe Lights 
Sirens and strobe lights are identified as highly effective tools for drawing 
attention to a security breach.  
Outdoor Sirens 
Installing outdoor sirens with a loud, attention-grabbing sound is essential 
for alerting neighbors and passersby in the event of a security breach. The 
security system can trigger these sirens remotely or automatically, 
ensuring swift attention to potential threats. 
Strobe Light Enhancement 
According to experts pairing outdoor sirens with flashing strobe lights for 
an additional visual deterrent can increase security. The combination of 
lights and sound can disorient and frighten intruders, encouraging them to 
abandon their attempted break-in. 
 9. Panic Buttons and Duress Codes 
Panic buttons and duress codes can be a secret lifeline during an 
emergency. To fully benefit from these features, follow the tips below.  
Accessible Placement 
Panic buttons should be installed in easily accessible locations to enable 
quick summoning of help during crises. Ideal locations include near the 
bed or main entrance, where they can be readily reached when needed 
most.

offers a non-lethal means of self-defense.  
Whistle Keychains 
Whistles are simple yet effective personal safety devices. Attaching a

threatened or in need of assistance. Blowing the whistle can attract

Once disaster has struck and looters and raiding parties begin targeting 
neighborhoods, they’ll start systematically going after individual homes. 
Any party of looters who are smart will analyze your home to determine its 
most vulnerable points before moving forward.  
That’s why understanding the areas that looters frequently target 
empowers you to implement effective measures for fortification of those 
specific areas. In this chapter, we will explore the primary places where 
looters seek access first.  
Front Door: A Gateway of Opportunity  
Let’s begin with the front door, a favored point of entry for looters due to its 
accessibility.  
While the front door may seem 
like an obvious entry point for 
burglars and looters, the truth is 
you’d be surprised by how many 
burglars take place each year 
where the burglars merely walk 
in through the front door after 
managing to get through the 
lock.  
Strengthening security of your front door requires careful consideration 
and the adoption of prudent measures, such as: 
Upgrading the Door  
Opt for a robust solid core wood or metal door, as it offers superior 
resistance against forced entry compared to hollow doors.

Sliding Glass Doors: A Weak Link  
Looters often target sliding glass doors due to their inherent vulnerability. 
Protecting against such threats necessitates proactive security 
enhancements: 
Implementing Security Bars or Rods 
Installing security bars or a metal 
rod within the door's track 
obstructs attempts at forced entry. 
When looters encounter these 
barriers, they'll realize that sliding 
the door open won't be simple. 
Utilizing Pin Locks and Anti-Lift Devices 
Employ pin locks and anti-lift devices to prevent the door from being lifted 
off its track, minimizing the risk of unauthorized access. These small but 
effective measures can make a big difference in securing sliding doors.

discourage potential intruders. If looters can't see what's inside, they

38 
Securing Valuables 
Keep valuables out of sight, whether inside the car or nearby. Pop them in 
the glove compartment or trunk to discourage looters from attempting 
theft. Don't make your car an attractive target by leaving valuable items in 
plain view. 
Unsecured Outdoor Valuables: Attracting Looters  
Outdoor valuables like bicycles, grills, and lawn equipment can tempt 
looters to either take those items or investigate your home further. 
Ensuring their security involves proactive protection: 
Utilizing Reliable Bike Locks 
Employ sturdy bike locks, securing bicycles to fixed structures like bike 
racks or posts, deterring theft attempts. Locking bikes prevents looters 
from easily snatching them. 
Safeguarding Portable Grills 
Lock up portable grills when not in use or store them within locked sheds 
or garages, reducing their vulnerability to theft. A locked grill is a grill 
looters can't walk away with. 
Anchoring Large Outdoor Equipment 
Anchor lawnmowers and generators to the ground, impeding looters from 
easily removing these valuable items. Securing large equipment makes it 
less appealing to potential thieves.

Your home should appear average, but be stronger than it looks.  The less 
attention you attract, the less likely you are to be selected. 
Set Up Deterrents  
Setting up warning signs like we discussed before is only the first step in 
deterring criminals or looters from proceeding to attack your home.  
The following measures will also be highly effective against deterring 
attackers: 
Lighting 
Many burglars like to take advantage of the shadows to keep themselves 
concealed. By installing strategic outside lighting, you can do much to 
make your home look much less appealing to attack.  
Set both the outside and inside of your home’s lights on a vacation timer 
so they will switch on automatically at regular intervals. This will create 
the appearance that somebody is home even when no one is. 
You can also set up motion sensor night lights like we discussed earlier in 
this book, so the lights will automatically flicker on when somebody walks 
past them.  
Noises 
Setting up noises is an excellent way to startle and discourage a burglar or 
a raider from continuing to try to break into your home.

For example, you can use a motion-activated sensor alarm that will create 
noise when it senses someone walking past. 
Another idea is to use a barking dog alarm that will create the noise of a 
dog barking inside the house when motion is detected outside of the 
house.  
Speaking of dogs… 
Get a Guard Dog  
Having a “beware of guard dog” sign is a great way to deter many people 
from breaking into your home, but having an actual guard dog takes the 
deterrence to a whole new level.  
Set Up Security Cameras  
Like we discussed earlier in this book as well, setting up security cameras 
are sure to give any intruder second thoughts, even if the cameras are not 
actually real.  
Set Up Barriers  
The above deterrents will work to keep some people at bay. But the more 
determined crooks and looters will not be phased by a barking dog or a 
security lighting or noise system.  
For these kinds of intruders who are more determined and desperate to 
break in, you’ll need to rely on actual physical barriers to keep them at bay.

Mark the burial site with a rock (or something else that you will remember

Tips to Reinforce Your Outside Doors  
All doors that are leading outside of your home should be reinforced so 
they are very difficult to break into. 
Most doors to homes are built out of wood, and while energy efficient and 
cheap to manufacture, they are also easy to break into. 
For example, if raiders come to your home armed with rifles or shotguns, 
there’s nothing to stop them from literally shooting through your door or 
beating it down with the stocks of their weapons.  
If they come with sledgehammers or mauls or axes, there’s nothing to 
really stop them from physically breaking down the door as well. 
You need to replace your doors leading outside so they can withstand a 
significant amount of trauma and force before being broken down.   
Doors made out of fiberglass, aluminum, or steel specifically will always 
be much more durable and harder to break into than standard wooden 
doors.

54 
Keep the following tips in mind to properly reinforce your doors leading 
outside: 
• Replace all doors leading outside with fiberglass, aluminum, or steel 
at the bare minimum  
• Replace all door hinges with heavy-duty door hinges (you can search 
for these online) 
• Replace all short screws in the strike plate of your doors with three-
inch screws  
• Make sure a peephole is installed in each door so you can see who 
is outside  
• Install heavy duty door knobs on all doors leading outside; make sure 
the lock is an ANSI (American National Standards Institute) Grade 1 
at the bare minimum  
• Make sure you have metal grates or grills installed behind the 
windows of any doors leading outside as well  
Use Door Jammers  
You can further reinforce your doors leading outside with the aid of door 
jammers or security bars. Make sure you have one door jammer per door.  
When the grid goes down and disaster strikes, you can take your jammers 
and install them behind each door.  
A door jammer makes it extremely difficult for anyone to break through a 
door. In the event that they manage to pick the lock to get the door open, 
for example, the jammer will provide an extra barrier of difficulty. 
If you don’t use a door jammer, an alternative is to use a door bar that you 
secure to both sides of the wall behind the door.

Reinforce Your Sliding Glass Doors  
While convenient and aesthetically appealing, sliding glass doors 
unfortunately provide a prime opportunity for someone to break into your 
home. 
In fact, it’s possible with certain types of sliding doors for someone to lift 
them up and out of the tracks from the outside. 
Take the following security measures with your sliding glass doors: 
• Make sure the glass itself to the doors is replaced with acrylic glass, 
which is a normal looking glass that is also much more difficult to 
physically break down with a higher impact resistance.  
• Install sliding door locks on both the bottom and the top of the door  
• Install double bolt locks to ensure the door cannot be physically 
lifted from the tracks 
• Place a wooden dowel in the track to prevent someone from sliding 
the door open after breaking through the lock. 
• The discussion of reinforcing your sliding glass window doors is a 
good segway into the next part of our discussion.  
Reinforce Your Windows  
After your doors, your windows are easily the most obvious entry point into 
your home, and if anything, they are even easier to break into.

56 
All an intruder has to do is physically break through a window (which they 
can do with a rifle stock or a rock) or pry it open to gain access. 
The easiest way to reinforce your windows is to reinforce them with acrylic 
glass such as Plexiglas. This will have much higher impact resistance for 
your doors while also not detracting from the look of your home in any way 
either.  
Make sure you do this with all windows to your home. While it is tempting 
to only reinforce the doors on the lower level of your home, criminals can 
still climb trees or ladders to access the higher windows. 
You can also install steel security bars behind your home as well for further 
reinforcement. While this may detract from the look of your home in daily 
life, reducing its property value or its curb appeal, you can have steel bars 
on hand that you can nail or screw into place after a major grid down 
disaster has struck.  
Steel bars are probably the most effective way to keep people from 
breaking through your windows, but in the event steel bars are not 
available you have other options as well. 
For example, you can take wooden boards or flat pieces of plywood and 
nail or screw them behind your windows as well. 
A determined looter armed with axes or hammers or rifles would likely be 
able to break through these, but they’ll have a much harder time of going 
about it than simply breaking through glass on its own, and it provides an 
additional barrier that they have to break through.  
Ultimately, anything that can slow down an intruder or raiding party from 
breaking into your home is to your benefit.

If you don’t have wooden boards or plywood available to nail behind your 
windows, the next best option is to just stack heavy boxes, sandbags, or 
even furniture behind your windows. 
Again, this defensive measure won’t keep the most determined of 
intruders from breaking all the way in, but it will still significantly slow them 
down and make it harder on their end to break in.  
Make Sure Your Valuables Are Secure  
While the above defensive measures we’ve discussed will be highly 
effective at making it more difficult for someone to break in, you always 
have to be prepared for the possibility that someone may succeed in 
breaking through. 
This is why you must take action to secure your valuable possessions 
inside of your home as well.  
Remember, the key to defending your home is to defend it in layers. The 
above measures we’ve discussed were about preventing access to your 
home from the outside. 
You also need to take measures to further defend your home from the 
inside as well. This starts with learning how to protect and hide your most 
valuable possessions. 
Remember, most burglars and looters are not going to spend a great deal 
of time in your home.  
They’ll want to get in and get out as quickly as they can for their own safety.

58 
valuables that they can take.  The trick is to not hide your valuables in 
obvious locations. 
For example, it’s a classic trick to hide jewelry in shoe boxes in a closet, 
rifles under a bed, or handguns under shirts and undergarments in a 
dresser drawer.  
Instead, you need to hide your valuables in the most unlikely of places.  
The master bedroom is usually the first room burglars and looters will 
search for valuables. This is why the master bedroom is the last place to 
store valuables such as jewelry, money, firearms, cash, or important 
documents. An office room in the home would be another obvious target.  
Consider hiding these kinds of items in a fireproof small safe, and then 
make an effort to hide that safe. One idea is to hide the safe in a container 
or box amongst a variety of other containers and boxes.  
Another idea is to hide your safe of valuables in the laundry room. The 
laundry room is arguably the one room that burglars overlook the most, 
because the only thing they imagine is in there are washing and drying 
machines and dirty clothes.  
Make Sure Your Food, Water, and Medications Are Secure  
In a grid down disaster situation, the biggest target for looters and raiders 
will be essentials such as food, water, and medications.   After the stores 
have all been looted, desperate people who need these items and are 
willing to rob to get them will turn to normal homes to get what they need. 
The same principles for storing your food and water apply to storing your 
valuables as well. Storing all of your food and water in the garage, kitchen, 
or pantry are poor options because they are already obvious.

59 
While some of your food will be stored in your pantry and kitchen for 
obvious reasons and for convenience in everyday life, you should also 
make an effort to store some of your food throughout your home as well.  
For example, you can hide food and water underneath beds, in closets, in 
a hidden safe room, or underneath the floorboards if you have a 
compartment under the floors.  
The idea is that if the intruders find and steal some of your food and water, 
you’ll still have food and water stored in other locations that you can turn 
to.  
Additional places where you could hide food, water, and medications 
include: 
• Inside travel suitcases or moving boxes 
• Buried outside somewhere in the yard  
• In a detached shop or shed that you have on your property (this is 
another obvious location, but again, the idea is to diversify where you 
keep your necessities) 
• Inside walls (this will require modification) 
• In cabinets all throughout your home (again, diversifying where you 
store your essentials is key) 
• Inside old appliances  
Pretend That You Are the Intruder  
Arguably the best method to identify potential vulnerabilities in your home 
is to view it through the eyes of an intruder. 
In other words, pretend that you are the intruder.

• It must have enough space to house everyone in your family; it might 
be cramped, but there should be enough space for people to rest and 
sleep (consider placing bunk beds in the room for this reason) 
• There should be at least a three days’ supply of food, water, and 
medications (such as prescription meds, if applicable) 
• There must be communication devices so you can get in touch with 
the outside world  
• It must have weapons (both non -lethal and lethal) that you can use 
to defend yourself in the event that someone breaks in 
• It must be in a location of the home that everyone can fleet to if 
necessary  
A common trick is for people to convert walk -in closets into their safe 
rooms. Most walk -in closets contain enough space to house entire 
families along with supplies and sleeping spaces to keep everyone alive 
and comfortable. 
The trick is you have to modify your home so the entrance into the walk-in 
space is hidden. For example, you can hide the entrance behind a fake 
bookshelf, or you can modify the walls so it appears as if there is no 
entrance.  
Another good trick is to create the safe room underneath the staircase, 
with the entrance to the room being one of the stairs that can flip open.  
The Importance of Fortifying Your Home  
Securing your home with the above tips is vital to ensuring that your home 
is more difficult to break into.

For example, most burglars are acutely aware of the practice of hiding a 
gun in a dresser drawer or jewelry or money in a shoebox or a rifle or a 
shotgun under the bed.  
Get more creative with where you hide your valuables. This goes for guns, 
ammunition, important documents, money, jewelry, family heirlooms, 
medals, and so on.  
Master bedrooms and offices are usually prime targets of where burglars 
and looters will look for such valuables.  
For instance, you could secure your jewelry in a fire-resistant safe deposit 
box, and then stash that box in an obscure location (such as a secret 
compartment in your home or in the laundry room, which is a room that 
many burglars will overlook). 
Leaving Valuables Out in The Open  
Leaving valuable items such as ladders, lawn mowers, or other ‘toys’ 
outside can make your home much more vulnerable to attack or a burglary 
because it will be more appealing.  
The best approach is to make sure that the outside of your home is kept 
clean and spotless outside. 
Not Forming a Defensive Perimeter Around Your Property

81 
In a grid down disaster scenario, your number one goal when it comes to 
home defense should be to keep armed raiding parties as far away from 
your home as possible. 
This underscores the critical importance of investing in a good defensive 
perimeter around your home.  
A barbed wire fence like we talked about in detail in this book previously 
alone will make your home far more defensible than most other defensive 
measures that are out there.  
This can be by either wrapping barbed wire around an existing fence or 
constructing a new barbed wire fence from the ground up.  
A good alternative to setting up a fence as a perimeter around your 
property is to rely on thorny bushes and brush.  
Having rose bushes around your home, for instance, can increase its 
property value and/or curb appeal in everyday life while also deterring 
burglars from coming in. 
Not Having Deterrents  
Ideally you can defend your home in a grid down disaster without resorting 
to violence. The best way to do this is to use deterrents to dissuade anyone 
from attempting to loot or break into your home.  This is why not having 
deterrents to your home can actually increase the odds of finding yourself 
in a violent conflict with an intruder.  
Examples of natural deterrents include, but are not limited to: 
• Warning Signs  
• Motion-Activated Lights 
• Motion-Activated Sounds

and determined burglars and raiders are turned away from attempting to 
attack or invade your home.  
As a result, you can decrease the odds of having to resort to violence to 
ensure the defense of yourself and your family.  
Not Having an Alert System   
Not having an alert system will be a major mistake because it means that 
you may not be able to detect danger when it is hovering right over you. 
Invest in something like a motion -activated camera that can alert you 
when there is anyone on your property. 
In the event that electronics and power are knocked out (such as from a 
solar flare, EMP attack, or a natural disaster) you may have to rely on more 
primitive methods to alert you to danger. 
Simply creating a perimeter of cordage around your property and then tying 
soda or beer cans filled with pebbles to the cordage is one way to alert you 
to the threat of danger. 
Having an alert guard dog is another good strategy.

When looters and raiding parties break into your home, they’ll immediately 
start scavenging for food, water, medicine, personal hygiene items, and 
whatever other supplies or items of value they can find.  
There’s an old saying to never keep your eggs all in one basket and that’s 
very applicable here. 
Don’t store all of your food and water in the pantry or in one location. 
Instead, store your food and water throughout the house and property and 
get creative with where you store it. 
What if you stored boxes of food behind the washing machine in the 
laundry room? Or what if you buried some food in a container outside?  
You get the idea. In the event your home is broken into during a grid down 
disaster, it would be catastrophic if literally all of your food was discovered 
and taken.  
The best way to avoid this is by diversifying where you store your food in 
the first place. 
Not Reinforcing Your Sliding Glass Doors  
Sliding glass doors are a favorite target for burglars to break into homes, 
and for good reason: they are incredibly easy to break down. 
That’s why failing to break down your sliding glass doors can prove to be a 
very serious mistake. Fortunately, you can greatly improve the security of 
your sliding glass doors with the following two preventative measures: 
• Replace the glass with acrylic glass 
• Add a doorstop over the rail

If your home comes under attack during a grid down disaster, looters may 
attempt to shoot at you through the windows. 
This is why you should invest in sandbags that you can stack behind your 
windows so you are provided with suitable cover from incoming gunfire. 
Not setting up sandbags in this manner could prove to be a fatal mistake. 
Failing to Lock the Doors and Windows 
It’s amazing how common this mistake actually is, and it’s one that can 
prove to be very costly. You have to get into the habit of ensuring that every 
door to your home is locked when you leave the home. 
Make sure that each of your family members and any other people living in 
the house are doing the same thing.  
Hiding Keys in Obvious Hiding Locations  
Ideally you won’t keep any keys to the house outside of the home other 
than on your person. But if you don’t like the idea of not having a way to get 
back into your house in the event you lose the keys you have on you, you 
need to be extremely strategic about where you place your hidden keys. 
Hiding your keys under a flower pot or the doormat is a well -known ‘trick’ 
to burglars and two places where they will look first when attempting to 
look for house keys.  
With that in mind, be more creative with where you place your keys. For 
example, you can bury your keys a few inches under the ground in the front 
or back yard and mark the spot with a small rock.  
Not Having a Safe Room in Your Home

It’s important to have a safe room in your home as a last resort place where 
you can go in the event your home is broken into and defense has become 
untenable.  
A safe room is simply any secret room in your home that houses enough 
space for your family to be safe and enough food and water to last you for 
three days.  
Not having a safe room, and specifically not having a safe room with 
enough room for your family and supplies, can prove to be a big mistake in 
the event that things make a move for the worst.  
Not Having an Escape Route 
Last but not least, always ensure you have an escape route to get out of 
your home, if need be, during a grid down disaster. 
Have a car ready to go, with supplies ready to be moved into the car to 
sustain yourself while you are on the go, and make sure that your defensive 
perimeter that you’ve made outside hasn’t completely boxed you in.  
If you have a barbed wire fence for your defensive perimeter, for instance, 
make sure you have a gate or some means of making a quick escape if you 
need to.
